desc:
A control panel is a grid of lamps; lamps[r][c] is 1 if that lamp is on and 0 if it is off. Every lamp is also a button. Pressing the button at (r, c) toggles that lamp and each of its orthogonal neighbours (up, down, left, right, when they exist): lamps that were on go off and lamps that were off go on.

Return the minimum number of button presses needed to turn every lamp off, or -1 if it is impossible.

lamps = [[0,0],[0,1]]     -> 3
lamps = [[1,0,1]]         -> 2   (press the two outer lamps)
lamps = [[1,0,0],[1,0,0]] -> -1
hints: What matters about the panel at any moment? Is there a compact way to describe the entire state?
The state is one of at most 2<sup>12</sup> = 4,096 on/off patterns, so it fits in a 12-bit integer. A press is an XOR with a fixed mask. Pressing the same button twice cancels out.

BFS over states: start from the initial pattern, apply every button mask with XOR, and stop when the pattern becomes 0. If the queue runs dry, return -1. Return 0 right away when everything is already off.
editorial: Encode the panel as a bitmask, bit r * cols + c being the lamp at (r, c). Each button has a fixed mask (its own bit plus the bits of its neighbours), and pressing it replaces the state s by s ^ mask. This turns the puzzle into an unweighted shortest-path problem on at most 4,096 states, with one edge per button from each state.

A breadth-first search from the starting pattern finds the fewest presses to reach the all-zero pattern. Keep a set (or array) of visited patterns so that every state is expanded once. The cost is states × buttons, at most 4,096 × 12.

Because pressing the same button twice cancels, order does not matter and every button is used at most once in an optimal solution, so enumerating all 2<sup>buttons</sup> subsets also works for these sizes. BFS is the version that generalises when presses interact in more complicated ways.
